newsitem.title: GREECE: Athens angry at EU efforts on Greek-Turkish talks.
newsitem.headline: Athens angry at EU efforts on Greek-Turkish talks.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said on Saturday the European Union was pushing too hard in its efforts for a Greek-Turkish rapprochement and advised the Dutch presidency to be more cautious.

"I have to observe that the course the presidency has opted exceeds her mandate and is liable to deny any usefulness from the initiative that we have tried to promote," Pangalos said in a letter to Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo.

The letter, dated May 16 and published in the Greek press on Saturday, was in response to an invitation by Van Mierlo for Greek and Turkish experts to meet in the Netherlands this month and seek ways to resolve longstanding differences.

Although both NATO members, the two countries have at times come close to war -- most recently in January 1996 over ownership of two uninhabited islets in the Aegean Sea. Other bones of contention are the divided island of Cyprus and the rights of a Moslem minority in northern Greece.

Pangalos rejected the proposed meeting as premature and said the experts should first exchange texts with the positions of both countries, something he had told Van Mierlo in earlier exchanges. The Netherlands currently holds the EU's rotating presidency.

"Greece has made clear from the start that the initiative at hand is neither a political dialogue nor an arbitration," Pangalos said in the letter. "I am sure that our purpose will be served better...if a more cautious approach would have been taken."

Greece and Turkey last month agreed to each set up a committee of experts to discuss bilateral problems, including rights in the Aegean. But Socialist Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis came under intense pressure from senior members of his party who said they would not endorse any negotiations with Ankara.
The Athens government then said the two committees would not meet face-to-face, but exchange letters with their views through the EU.
"We are about ready to send the text (with the Greek positions) on condition that this request for a meeting be withdrawn, as it creates problems to the whole procedure," Pangalos told reporters.

He said Greece would accept no pressure from the EU to start negotiations and that any rapprochement with Turkey now did not mean Athens would lift its veto within the EU blocking millions of dollars in aid to Ankara.

To lift its veto, Greece wants Turkey to publicly renounce force as a way to settle disputes, abide by international laws and treaties on existing borders, and agree to settle differences through international courts.

Despite the setback over the experts' meeting, it is the first time since last year's military standoff that the two neighbours have considered talking to each other even through letters to a third body.
